extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduate and graduate students in mathematics; researchers interested in rigorous proofs in algebra, combinatorial geometry, and analysis
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and constructive techniques for producing and checking rigorous mathematical proofs (e.g., Monsky’s theorem, valuation constructions, Pólya’s projection theorem). Emphasizes precise definitions, constructive colorings, valuation/ring arguments, counting parity arguments, and analytic reductions (cosine polynomials/Chebyshev).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of non-Archimedean valuation (values in ordered abelian group)
rubrics_metrics.description: A valuation v: K → {0} ∪ G (G an ordered abelian group) must satisfy: (i) v(x)=0 ⇔ x=0; (ii) v(xy)=v(x)v(y); (iii) v(x+y) ≤ max{v(x),v(y)}; (iv) v(x+y)=max{v(x),v(y)} whenever v(x) ≠ v(y).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This version uses only multiplicative structure and order on values (no additive structure of R>0 required). Consequences noted: if v(x)<1 and x≠0 then v(x^{-1}) = v(x)^{-1} > 1. This definition and these consequences are used as the technical foundation for Monsky’s coloring argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence/characterization of valuation rings via K = R ∪ R^{-1}
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a valuation v, its valuation ring is R := {x ∈ K : v(x) ≤ 1} and units U := {x : v(x)=1}. A proper subring R ⊆ K is a valuation ring for some valuation iff K = R ∪ R^{-1}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use quotient group G := K^×/U and define order xU < yU ⇔ xy^{-1} ∈ R\U to recover v. This provides a constructive route from rings to valuations (used in the appendix to build the needed valuation on R).

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructing a valuation on R with v(1/2) > 1 (strategy via maximal subring)
rubrics_metrics.description: To obtain a valuation on R with v(1/2)>1 it suffices to find a subring B ⊂ R not containing 1/2 that is maximal with respect to this property; such a maximal subring B is a valuation ring and yields the desired valuation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Existence of maximal B follows from Zorn's lemma (chain union). To prove maximal B is a valuation ring, show that if α ∈ R \ (B ∪ B^{-1}) then extending by α contradicts maximality via polynomial expressions in α and α^{-1} with coefficients in B (explicitly use representations like 1 = 2u0 + 2u1α + ...). The proof uses minimality arguments on polynomial degrees to get a contradiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coloring rule based on valuation-maximal coordinate
rubrics_metrics.description: Color each point (x,y) ∈ R^2 by examining (x,y,1) and taking the first coordinate (in order x, y, 1) in which the valuation v attains its maximum: blue if the first maximal coordinate is x (v(x) ≥ v(y), v(x) ≥ v(1)), green if first maximal is y (v(x)<v(y), v(y) ≥ v(1)), red if first maximal is the 1 (v(x)<v(1), v(y)<v(1)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This assigns a unique color to every point. The coloring is the key constructive device in Monsky’s theorem: it makes algebraic v-value comparisons translate into combinatorial color constraints. Example: figure shows colors on a grid of rationals k/20.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma: determinant v-value ≥ 1 for blue/green/red triple
rubrics_metrics.description: For a blue point pb=(xb,yb), green pg=(xg,yg), and red pr=(xr,yr), the valuation v of the 3×3 determinant det[[xb,xg,xr],[yb,yg,yr],[1,1,1]] is at least 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof idea: main diagonal summand x_b y_g ·1 has v-value ≥1 because each diagonal entry has maximal v-value in its row; other five summands have strictly smaller v-values. Use property (iv) of non-Archimedean valuations to conclude the determinant’s v-value equals the main diagonal’s v-value (hence ≥1). This is the algebraic backbone that translates coloring to area constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary: any line has at most two colors; rainbow triangle area constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: No line in the plane receives all three colors (at most two). A triangle with vertices of three different colors (‘rainbow triangle’) cannot be degenerate (area 0) and its Euclidean area cannot equal 1/n for odd n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translate the triangle area (half the determinant of Lemma 1) into valuation bounds: determinant cannot be 0 since v(0)=0, and if area were 1/n for odd n then valuation properties produce a contradiction with Lemma 1 (v(1/2)>1 implies contradictions in v-values of ±2/n etc.). This links combinatorial coloring to arithmetic impossibility of equal-area odd dissections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parity-counting criterion via red–blue segments (Sperner-inspired)
rubrics_metrics.description: In any finite triangulation (dissection) of the unit square into triangles, consider red–blue segments (edges connecting red and blue vertices). The bottom boundary forces an odd number of red–blue boundary segments; interior segments are counted twice across triangles. Triangles with ≤2 colors contribute an even number of red-blue boundary edges, while rainbow triangles contribute an odd number. Summing across all triangles yields an odd total count, hence an odd number of rainbow triangles appears in the dissection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the combinatorial counting argument (Sperner’s lemma flavor) that turns the coloring’s local constraints into a global parity conclusion ensuring at least one rainbow triangle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sperner-style argument / strategy for deriving contradiction in geometric dissections
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a specially constructed coloring with local line constraints and a parity argument counting color-change edges to show that any dissection must contain an object (rainbow triangle) forbidden by the algebraic valuation property, yielding a contradiction when assuming an odd equal-area dissection exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This meta-criterion summarizes the proof strategy: combine an algebraically designed invariant (valuation-based coloring) with combinatorial topology (parity/counting) to preclude certain geometric decompositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Zorn’s Lemma to construct maximal substructures
rubrics_metrics.description: To build an algebraic object maximal with a property (e.g., a subring B ⊂ R not containing 1/2), use Zorn’s Lemma: any chain has an upper bound (union), so a maximal element exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a standard existence technique in algebraic constructions; the text emphasizes checking the chain upper bound preserves the property (not containing 1/2) and then using maximality to deduce structural properties (valuation ring).

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of the ordered value group from units: G = K^×/U with order via R\U
rubrics_metrics.description: Given valuation ring R and its unit subgroup U, form the quotient multiplicative group G = K^×/U and define xU < yU iff xy^{-1} ∈ R\U; then v(x)=xU (for x≠0) recovers the valuation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provides a canonical algebraic construction linking subrings/units to valuation value groups; useful when only multiplicative/order structure is needed (as in Monsky’s proof). Verify (i)–(iii) hold for this v.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chebyshev’s theorem as an analytic extremal criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: For real polynomials p(x) of degree n with leading coefficient 1, max_{−1≤x≤1} |p(x)| ≥ 1/2^{n−1}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use cosine-polynomial representation g(θ)=p(cos θ), express cos^k θ as cosine polynomials, and show the leading cosine coefficient bn = 1/2^{n−1}. Then show |bn| ≤ max|g(θ)| by evaluating sign changes at θ = kπ/n (Harmonic/oscillation argument). Chebyshev polynomials give equality cases and identify extremal polynomials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary: interval-length bound from Chebyshev
rubrics_metrics.description: If p(x) is monic degree n and |p(x)| ≤ 2 on an interval [a,b], then b−a ≤ 4.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rescale the interval to [−1,1] and apply Chebyshev’s bound; this quantitative control on the length of connected subsets where |p| ≤ 2 is a key step in Pólya’s projection theorem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pólya’s reduction: reduce complex polynomial projection problem to real-root polynomials
rubrics_metrics.description: Given f(z)=z^n + ... and C={z:|f(z)|≤2}, project C to the real axis. If p(x) = ∏(x − a_k) uses the real parts of roots, then R (projection) is contained in P={x:|p(x)|≤2}; proving P can be covered by intervals of total length ≤4 suffices to prove the original projection bound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reduction relies on |x−a_k| ≤ |z − c_k| so |p(x)| ≤ |f(z)|. It transforms a complex-analytic geometric bound into a real-polynomial inequality problem amenable to Chebyshev techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pólya’s interval-merging construction to maximize covered length
rubrics_metrics.description: Given p(x) with P = ∪ I_j, construct p1(x)=q(x+d) r(x) by shifting roots that lie in the rightmost interval by the gap d between It−1 and It; p1 then has set P1 covering I1 ∪ ... ∪ It−1 ∪ (It − d). Repeating merges intervals until you obtain a monolithic interval whose length at least equals total length of P.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This algorithmic polynomial modification increases (or at least does not decrease) the total covered length while preserving monicity; it is the constructive step that reduces the multi-interval case to the single-interval case where Chebyshev’s corollary applies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Facts about real-root polynomials used as proof tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Fact 1: If b is a multiple root of p'(x), then b is a root of p(x). Fact 2: For real-root polynomial p, p'(x)^2 ≥ p(x) p''(x) for all real x (proved via product/differentiation representation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These analytic/algebraic inequalities provide necessary sign/multiplicity control used when proving roots must lie inside intervals I_j and in arguments involving extrema within intervals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Littlewood–Offord / Sperner counting principle for combinatorial sums
rubrics_metrics.description: For scalar ai with |ai|≥1, the number of signed sums ∑ ε_i a_i that can lie in any interval (or circle) of radius 1 is at most the largest binomial coefficient ~ C(n,⌊n/2⌋) (with sharper bounds via Sperner’s theorem).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The real proof uses antichain arguments (distinct sign-index sets I form antichain), Sperner’s theorem upper bound, and Stirling for asymptotics. This is a combinatorial extremal criterion linking geometry of sums to set-systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kleitman’s vector-generalization counting criterion (induction on n)
rubrics_metrics.description: For vectors a_i in R^d with |a_i|≥1 and k bounded open regions of diameter <2, the number of signed sums lying in the union of those regions is at most the sum of the k largest binomial coefficients; in particular for k=1, at most the largest binomial coefficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof strategy: assume regions disjoint; use recursion of binomial coefficients and an induction step that partitions sums based on sign of ε_n and constructs bijections to sums for n−1 vectors lying in k±1 regions (uses a geometric claim about disjointness of certain translated regions). This gives tight combinatorial packing bounds in higher dimensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Herglotz trick / functional-equation identification strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: To identify two meromorphic/periodic functions (e.g., f(x)=π cot πx and g(x)=lim_{N→∞} ∑_{n=-N}^N 1/(x+n)) show they share key analytic/algebraic properties: continuity off poles, period 1, oddness, and the same functional equation (f(x/2)=2f(x) etc.), and that their difference extends continuously to all R (hence must be constant zero).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify (A) uniform convergence/local continuity; (B) periodicity by reorganizing sums; (C) oddness; (D) same scaling/functional equation. This method proves classical partial-fraction expansions by uniqueness of a function with those properties.
